analysis.one_liner: Allows the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set safety standards for guns and gun parts.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never received a committee vote or House floor vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal consumer product safety law currently excludes pistols, revolvers, and other firearms from the definition of a consumer product, which means the Consumer Product Safety Commission cannot write safety standards for guns the way it does for cribs, toys, or power tools. This bill would strike that exclusion, letting the Commission issue safety standards for firearms and firearm components.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy or use firearms and their families would gain a government safety regulator with authority over defective firearms and components, similar to the protection they already have for other household products.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the exclusion of pistols, revolvers, and other firearms from the Consumer Product Safety Act's definition of 'consumer product,' placing guns under the same consumer product safety regime as other household goods.
Gives the Consumer Product Safety Commission authority to issue safety standards for firearms and firearm components.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and firearm-component manufacturers and importers would bear the cost of complying with any safety standards the Commission issues, and consumers could face some of those costs in gun prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance with new safety standards would raise costs for firearm manufacturers, costs that could be passed on to buyers, and small gunmakers would face proportionally heavier compliance burdens.

Critics of the change have long argued that giving a product-safety agency authority over firearms could be used not just to fix defects but to set standards so restrictive that some firearms could no longer be lawfully made or sold, effectively regulating guns out of the market rather than making them safer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest in scope: it would not ban or restrict guns, it would simply let an existing safety agency act when a specific model is defective, the way it does for other products. The cost falls on an industry that currently faces no federal product-safety oversight at all. The main honest objection is the risk that safety rulemaking could become a back door to restricting lawful gun ownership, which is a matter of how the authority would be used rather than what the bill literally does.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then a subcommittee, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the bill on June 21, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where it stayed.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors, and no further action was ever taken on it.
Because Congress adjourned on January 3, 2025, the bill died without ever receiving a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm and firearm-component manufacturers came out ahead: they keep their exemption from consumer product safety law, so no federal agency can issue mandatory safety standards for firearms. Gun consumers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearm manufacturers keeping their safety-law exemption

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give the Consumer Product Safety Commission authority over firearms.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce and took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Gun-rights organizations and the firearms industry
against.role: Outside opposition to CPSC jurisdiction over firearms
against.what_they_did: Long-standing, well-documented opposition to giving the Consumer Product Safety Commission any authority over firearms, on the grounds that it could be used to restrict gun availability.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and only one member of either party supported the bill, so the partisan shape of a real fight never showed itself; the lone sponsor was a Democrat and the bill drew zero cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would end their unique exemption from consumer product safety law, exposing them to mandatory safety standards and recalls for defective products for the first time. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against gun buyers, who currently have no federal safety regulator for defective firearms.

Retailers would face a modest compliance burden and possible recalls of stock, but also benefit from clearer liability lines if products meet safety standards. Their trade groups have historically opposed any CPSC role over guns.
